spans.content: Deep Learning Networks for View-independent Knee and Elbow Joint
Angle Estimation
Ankhzaya Jamsrandorj, Konki Sravan Kumar, Muhammad Zeeshan Arshad, Kyung-Ryoul Mun, Jinwook Kim
Abstract— Vision-based human joint angle estimation is es-
sential for remote and continuous health monitoring. Most
vision-based angle estimation methods use the locations of
human joints extracted using optical motion cameras, depth
cameras, or human pose estimation models. This study aimed
to propose a reliable and straightforward approach with deep
learning networks for knee and elbow flexion/extension angle
estimation from the RGB video. Fifteen healthy participants
performed four daily activities in this study. The experiments
were conducted with four different deep learning networks,
and the networks took nine subsequent frames as input while
output was knee and elbow joint angles extracted from an
optical motion capture system for each frame. The BiLSTM
network-based joint angles estimator can estimate both joint
angles with a correlation of 0.955 for knee and 0.917 for elbow
joints regardless of the camera view angles.
I. INTRODUCTION
Continuous estimation of human joint angles enables
critical clinical analysis for injury risk in the elderly, the
effect of rehabilitation after surgery, and diagnosis and assess
human joint movement disorders. The knee flexion/extension
and elbow flexion/extension angles in the daily living ac-
tivity can serve as indicators of the level of neurological
and musculoskeletal disorders such as Parkinson’s disease,
stroke, frailty, and cerebral palsy. Therefore, accurate and
reliable knee and elbow joint angle estimation is essential
for appropriate clinical intervention.
Wearable sensors such as surface electromyography
(sEMG) and inertial measurement unit (IMU) are widely
used for their high accuracy and capability to remotely mon-
itor human motion outside the lab to estimate human joint
angles. However, wearable sensor-based methods require the
professionals to attach the sensors to the participant’s body,
analyze the output signals, and cooperate highly with the
participants [1]–[5]. On the other hand, vision-based methods
are used for human joint angle estimation. Current vision-
based methods mainly use data generated by specialized
hardware or software such as optical motion cameras, depth
cameras, passive marker-based systems, or human pose esti-
mators [6]–[12]. Schmitz et al. proposed a markerless motion
capture system for evaluating the accuracy of joint angles
measured using a single camera. The system collected the
depth map and 2D images of a testing jig using the Kinect
camera. An articulated iterative closest point algorithm as-
suming a ball-and-socket joint at the knee was used to align
these captured data with the template. Then, the system
exported the virtual marker trajectories, and the joint angles
were calculated using these trajectories [7]. Wang et al.
proposed a computer-vision method to estimate joint angles
during lifting tasks using a single camera, and the method
estimated the joint angles in three steps. First, the videos
were preprocessed in Detectron2 to detect 2D key points of
human joints in each frame. Then the VideoPose3D model
reconstructed the 3D pose using 2D key points. Finally, the
joint angles were calculated by a top-down inverse dynamic
biomechanics model using 3D joint coordinates [10]. Kidzin-
ski et al. designed a machine learning model to predict the
clinical gait metrics. They extracted the 2D body poses from
videos using OpenPose. These human pose trajectories were
fed into a neural network to estimate the knee flexion angle
at maximum extension [11]. These vision-based methods
entirely depend on human joint’s location extracted by using
the depth-sensing cameras, passive markers tracking system,
or human pose estimation models. However, the coverage
area of the depth cameras is limited, and the illumination
conditions of the environment can substantially impact the
estimation accuracy in human joint angles. Besides, the
extracted joint locations by the human pose detection system
may not be the center of that joints, and this can affect
joint angle estimation results. Kumar et al. proposed a video-
based system using deep learning techniques to address the
limitations of the vision-based methods mentioned above.
A deep convolutional neural network trained with a stack of
few video frames estimated the angular velocity of the human
lower limb during walking on the treadmill and squat [13].
Inspired by [13], this study aimed to propose a simple,
practical, and multi-view approach of using deep learning
networks for the knee flexion/extension and elbow flex-
ion/extension angle estimation.

II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
A. Participants
This study is based on work supported by the Institutional
Review Board of the Korea Institute of Science and Tech-
nology.
A total of 15 participants (12 males and 3 females; age =
24.2 ±3.8 years, height = 170.7 ±6.4 cm, and weight = 71.7
±16.1 kg) without any history or presence of neurological
disorders participated in this experiment. All participants
provided written informed consent and no violation was
made during the experiment.

B. Experimental protocol
The data was collected from an indoor environment with
a video system and a motion capture system, as shown in
Fig.1, and the capture area had a size of 3.68 and 2.0 meters.
The motion capture system had six optical motion cameras,
which tracked the position of the markers attached to the
participant’s both knees and elbows, and the motion capture
data was assembled at a sampling frequency of 120Hz. While
timely-synchronized 4 RGB cameras simultaneously cap-
tured the video data with a resolution of Full HD and a frame
rate of 60 Hz. A flash-based synchronization method was
developed to generate the pulses lasting 100ms in the optical
data while the digital cameras capture the flash moment. The
optical motion and digital cameras were synchronized using
these flash signals for each participant and each action trial.
The participants were instructed to perform four daily
actions: Squat, Walking in place (WIP), One leg stand (OLS),
and Arm. For the Squat activity, the participants squatted for
30 seconds. The participants were asked to walk in place at a
self-selected pace in the WIP action. For the OLS activity, the
participants stood on one leg and lifted another, and repeated
it for the opposite leg. The participants were instructed to
hold both arms parallel to the ground and bend them at the
elbow. Then extend arms out to the sides, bring them to
the initial pose, push the arms to the front, and return them.
Participants repeated this for a minute while standing upright
for the Arm action. Finally, a total of 1.29M frames were
included in the dataset. The dataset details are summarized
in Table I. Ground-truth metrics of both knee and elbow
joint angles were computed from optical motion capture data.
Each video is provided with human bounding boxes on every
frame and an annotation containing the four angles: the right
and left knee flexion/extension and the right and left elbow
flexion/extension.
C. Knee and elbow angle estimator development
The architecture of the proposed network was composed of
two parts: A feature extraction model and an LSTM-based
joint angles estimator. Fig.2 shows the architecture of the
LSTM-based estimator proposed in this study. We adopted
the ResNet18 pre-trained on ImageNet as the backbone fea-
ture extractor and took the nine subsequent frames as input.

and Elbow angles by four different deep learning networks
during the Squat and WIP actions, respectively. The Knee
and the Elbow angle estimation results while performing the
OLS and Arm actions were illustrated in Fig.5 and Fig.6,

Table II summarized the MAE and PCC of the deep learn-

and the right and left elbow flexion/extension angles. The

IV. DISCUSSION
This study proposed a novel approach of using deep
learning networks to estimate the knee flexion/extension and
elbow flexion/extension angles. The deep learning networks
trained with a few subsequent video frames achieved promis-
ing performance, besides the simple 2D network trained
with a single frame likewise achieved satisfactory results
in estimating the knee and elbow joint angles regardless of
camera view angles. It should be noted that this approach
does not require any special sensors, markers, and human
pose estimators for human joint angle estimation.
Deep learning networks estimated the joint angles with an
average MAE of 8.57 and an average PCC of 0.969 for the
knee joints and 14.05 and 0.900 for the elbow joints. Table
VI summarized the performance of the networks on different
camera view angles separately. The estimation performance
of the networks for the knee flexion/extension angles was
relatively good regardless of camera view angles. In contrast,

It was observed similarly from the opposite camera view.
As mentioned in the introduction section, most vision-
based methods used a particular camera system and human
pose estimation machines to locate human joints and track
them to estimate human joint angles. Cai et al. investigated
the accuracy of a single Kinect-based system in measur-
ing upper limb joint angles when Kinect sensor placed at
different distances and orientations. The upper limb joint
angles were calculated based on the 3D coordinates of the
trunk and upper limb joint center derived from the Kinect
v2 sensor during the upper limb functional task. For the
elbow joint angle estimation, the MAEs ranged from 10.20
to 28.32, depending on the placements of the Kinect sensor.
The Kinect-based system achieved the minimum MAE of
10.20 when the Kinect sensor was placed at 30° to the left
side for estimating the elbow flexion/extension angle [6].
Pantzar-Castilla et al. designed a system with an RGB-D
camera for the knee joint angle estimation from the side view.
The hip, knee, and ankle joints center were extracted from
depth data and tracked during walking. Then, the knee angles
were calculated using these joint center trajectories. The
system estimated the knee angles with an average correlation
of 0.906 [12]. Compared to these studies, our approach
achieved remarkable performance in estimating the knee
and elbow joint angle from the multi-camera view angles
without the special camera and human pose information. We
expect the proposed approach to serving as effective and
practical human joint angles estimation methods for remote
and continuous health monitoring.
This study has a limitation related to its generalizability.
The study participants were primarily young and healthy.
Therefore, applying our approach to the various participants
groups, including the elderly, patients with conditions such

IV. DISCUSSION
This study proposed a novel approach of using deep
learning networks to estimate the knee flexion/extension and
elbow flexion/extension angles. The deep learning networks
trained with a few subsequent video frames achieved promis-
ing performance, besides the simple 2D network trained
with a single frame likewise achieved satisfactory results
in estimating the knee and elbow joint angles regardless of
camera view angles. It should be noted that this approach
does not require any special sensors, markers, and human
pose estimators for human joint angle estimation.
Deep learning networks estimated the joint angles with an
average MAE of 8.57 and an average PCC of 0.969 for the
knee joints and 14.05 and 0.900 for the elbow joints. Table
VI summarized the performance of the networks on different
camera view angles separately. The estimation performance
of the networks for the knee flexion/extension angles was
relatively good regardless of camera view angles. In contrast,
camera view angles influenced the elbow flexion/extension
angles estimation. As shown in Table VI, the deep learning
networks estimated the elbow joint angles with higher MAE
from the backside due to unseeable elbow flexions during
the Squat and Arm actions. Accordingly, the networks
estimation errors were lesser on the right knee and elbow
joints than the left from the camera view of the right side.

As mentioned in the introduction section, most vision-
based methods used a particular camera system and human
pose estimation machines to locate human joints and track
them to estimate human joint angles. Cai et al. investigated
the accuracy of a single Kinect-based system in measur-
ing upper limb joint angles when Kinect sensor placed at
different distances and orientations. The upper limb joint
angles were calculated based on the 3D coordinates of the
trunk and upper limb joint center derived from the Kinect
v2 sensor during the upper limb functional task. For the
elbow joint angle estimation, the MAEs ranged from 10.20
to 28.32, depending on the placements of the Kinect sensor.
The Kinect-based system achieved the minimum MAE of
10.20 when the Kinect sensor was placed at 30° to the left
side for estimating the elbow flexion/extension angle [6].
Pantzar-Castilla et al. designed a system with an RGB-D
camera for the knee joint angle estimation from the side view.
The hip, knee, and ankle joints center were extracted from
depth data and tracked during walking. Then, the knee angles
were calculated using these joint center trajectories. The
system estimated the knee angles with an average correlation
of 0.906 [12]. Compared to these studies, our approach
achieved remarkable performance in estimating the knee
and elbow joint angle from the multi-camera view angles
without the special camera and human pose information. We
expect the proposed approach to serving as effective and
practical human joint angles estimation methods for remote
and continuous health monitoring.
This study has a limitation related to its generalizability.
The study participants were primarily young and healthy.
Therefore, applying our approach to the various participants
groups, including the elderly, patients with conditions such
as Parkinson’s disease, stroke, cerebral palsy, and muscular
dystrophy, is in the future work plan.

V. CONCLUSIONS
This study proposed a multi-view, vision-based approach
that does not require a special camera system and wear-
able sensors for joint angle estimation using deep learning
networks. The deep learning networks trained with a few
video frames showed outstanding performance in estimating
the knee and elbow joint angles regardless of camera view
angles. Our approach can be applied to monitor the people’s
health in their homes for early diagnosis of diseases, proper
treatment, and timely intervention.
